title: Child BMI Percentile Calculator (CDC) + chart | Hacé Cuentas
description: Find your child's BMI percentile by age and sex using CDC growth charts. Free, no sign-up needed and instant results.
answerSnippet: Child BMI is read by percentile for the child's age and sex, not by fixed adult cutoffs. Per the CDC (ages 2-19): below the 5th percentile is Underweight, 5th to <85th is Healthy Weight, 85th to <95th is Overweight, and ≥95th is Obesity. The 2023 AAP guideline adds Severe Obesity at ≥120% of the 95th percentile (or BMI ≥35). BMI is calculated as weight (kg) ÷ height (m)², or 703 × weight (lb) ÷ height (in)².
intro: Child **[BMI](/bmi-calculator)** is interpreted by **age- and sex-specific percentile**, not by the fixed adult cutoffs you may have seen for yourself. The reason is biological: a child's body composition shifts dramatically between ages 2 and 19 — fat mass dips during early childhood (the "adiposity rebound"), then rises again in puberty at different ages for boys and girls. A BMI value that's perfectly healthy for a 4-year-old can signal real risk in a 14-year-old, and vice versa. In US pediatric practice, the **CDC 2000 Growth Charts** are the standard reference for ages 2-19, while **WHO Growth Standards** are used from birth to age 2 (per AAP recommendation). The four CDC weight-status categories used by US pediatricians are: **Underweight (<5th percentile)**, **Healthy Weight (5th to <85th)**, **Overweight (85th to <95th)**, and **Obesity (≥95th)**. The **2023 AAP Clinical Practice Guideline on Obesity** also defined **Severe Obesity** as BMI ≥120% of the 95th percentile (or BMI ≥35 kg/m²), a threshold that triggers more intensive treatment options including pharmacotherapy and, in select adolescents, metabolic and bariatric surgery.
keyTakeaway: US pediatricians read child BMI by **CDC percentile (ages 2-19)**: **<5th = Underweight**, **5th-84th = Healthy Weight**, **85th-94th = Overweight**, **≥95th = Obesity**, **≥120% of the 95th = Severe Obesity** (2023 AAP guideline). One BMI number means nothing without age, sex, and the growth curve over time.
useCases: Well-child visit screening: confirm the BMI percentile your pediatrician plotted at the annual check-up and understand the CDC category.

Intervention tier decision: knowing whether your child crosses the 85th, 95th, or 120% of 95th percentile helps frame the conversation about Intensive Health Behavior and Lifestyle Treatment (IHBLT), pharmacotherapy eligibility, or surgical referral per the 2023 AAP guideline.
Pediatrician handoff prep: bring an accurate BMI percentile and trend to the visit so the appointment focuses on a plan, not on arithmetic.
School nurse height/weight screening: many US school districts run annual BMI screenings — use this to interpret the letter sent home and decide if a follow-up with the PCP is warranted.

Tracking comorbidity risk: a BMI percentile ≥95th raises the index of suspicion for type 2 diabetes, NAFLD, obstructive sleep apnea, dyslipidemia, and hypertension — useful before lab work is ordered.
Coaches and youth sports medicine: distinguish between athletic body composition and true elevated adiposity before recommending nutrition or training changes.

example.title: Example: 7-year-old boy, 55 lb (25 kg), 48 in (122 cm)
example.result: BMI: **16.8 kg/m²**. Percentile: **~75th** (Healthy Weight). Continue routine well-child monitoring; no intervention required.

explanation:
## The BMI formula is the same for kids — interpretation is not

The math is identical to the adult [BMI calculator](/bmi-calculator):

```
BMI (metric) = weight (kg) / height (m)²
BMI (US)    = 703 × weight (lb) / height (in)²
```

A child with a weight of 55 lb and a height of 48 in has a BMI of 703 × 55 / 48² ≈ 16.8 kg/m² — the same number you'd get with metric units. What changes for pediatrics is the **lookup**: instead of comparing to fixed adult cutoffs (18.5, 25, 30), you compare to the **CDC 2000 BMI-for-age growth chart** for the child's specific age and sex.

## CDC vs WHO charts — which one for a US child?

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends:

- **Birth to age 2**: use the **WHO Growth Standards** (based on breastfed infants under optimal conditions, considered the gold standard for early growth).
- **Ages 2-19**: use the **CDC 2000 Growth Charts** (based on a US reference population, the standard in US clinical practice and what your pediatrician's EHR will display).

This calculator follows that convention for ages 2-19.

## CDC weight-status categories (ages 2-19)

The Severe Obesity thresholds come from the **2023 AAP Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Treatment of Children and Adolescents with Obesity** (Hampl et al., *Pediatrics* 2023) and now drive intensive treatment decisions.

## Quick reference: BMI cutoffs by age and sex

These are approximate BMI values (kg/m²) at the key percentile lines for selected ages. Use them as a sanity check — your child's exact percentile depends on the full growth curve, which this calculator interpolates.

| Age | Sex | 5th (Underweight below) | 85th (Overweight at/above) | 97th (Obesity at/above) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 yr | Boy | 13.8 | 16.9 | 18.3 |
| 5 yr | Girl | 13.4 | 17.0 | 18.7 |
| 8 yr | Boy | 13.8 | 18.0 | 20.4 |
| 8 yr | Girl | 13.5 | 18.3 | 21.0 |
| 10 yr | Boy | 14.2 | 19.3 | 22.3 |
| 10 yr | Girl | 14.0 | 19.9 | 23.2 |
| 12 yr | Boy | 15.0 | 20.9 | 24.4 |
| 12 yr | Girl | 14.8 | 21.3 | 25.0 |
| 14 yr | Boy | 16.0 | 22.6 | 26.2 |
| 14 yr | Girl | 15.8 | 22.8 | 26.7 |
| 16 yr | Boy | 17.0 | 24.0 | 27.5 |
| 16 yr | Girl | 16.6 | 24.0 | 27.8 |
| 18 yr | Boy | 17.8 | 25.0 | 28.5 |
| 18 yr | Girl | 17.1 | 24.5 | 28.4 |

Notice how the same BMI lands in different categories at different ages: a BMI of 18 is **obese** for a 5-year-old boy but **healthy weight** for a 14-year-old boy. That is exactly why a single BMI number is meaningless for a child without age and sex.

## The 2023 AAP guideline — a major shift

The AAP's 2023 guideline reframed pediatric obesity as a **chronic disease** to be treated early and intensively, not watched and waited on:

- **Intensive Health Behavior and Lifestyle Treatment (IHBLT)** — ≥26 contact hours over 3-12 months — is the foundation for children 6+ with overweight or obesity.
- **Pharmacotherapy** can be offered as an adjunct to IHBLT for adolescents ≥12 years with obesity. Approved options include **semaglutide (Wegovy)**, **liraglutide (Saxenda)**, **phentermine/topiramate (Qsymia)**, and **orlistat**.
- **Metabolic and bariatric surgery** should be considered for adolescents ≥13 years with severe obesity (BMI ≥120% of 95th or ≥35 kg/m²) and referred to comprehensive multidisciplinary pediatric programs.

The guideline explicitly moved away from the prior "watchful waiting" approach.

## Comorbidity risk rises with percentile

Elevated pediatric BMI is associated with:

- **Type 2 diabetes** — screening recommended starting at age 10 with BMI ≥85th percentile plus one risk factor.
- **Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)** — now the leading cause of pediatric chronic liver disease in the US; ALT screening from age 9-11.
- **Obstructive sleep apnea** — snoring + obesity should trigger a sleep study referral.
- **Dyslipidemia** — universal lipid screening between ages 9-11 and again 17-21 per NHLBI.
- **Hypertension** — measure BP at every well-child visit from age 3.
- **Depression and anxiety** — screen routinely; weight stigma worsens outcomes.
- **Musculoskeletal complications** — slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), Blount's disease.

## Waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) as a complement

A growing body of evidence supports **waist-to-height ratio > 0.5** as a simple cardiometabolic screen in children, sometimes catching abdominal adiposity that BMI alone misses (the "normal-weight central obesity" phenotype). It's not a replacement for BMI percentile but a useful add-on, especially for muscular kids whose BMI may overestimate fat mass.

## Weight-bias prevention language

Use **person-first language**: "a child with obesity," not "an obese child." The AAP and Obesity Medicine Association both emphasize this — weight stigma in clinical encounters is documented to worsen physical and mental health outcomes and erode the therapeutic relationship. Avoid moralizing food ("junk," "bad") in front of the child; focus on family-wide behaviors, not individual blame.

## Parental and household factors

- **Modeling**: kids eat what they see parents eat. Family meals at the table (vs in front of a screen) are associated with healthier weight trajectories.
- **Screen time**: AAP recommends **no screens under 18 months** (except video chat), **<1 hour/day of high-quality programming for ages 2-5**, and **consistent limits 5+** with priority on sleep, physical activity, and offline interaction.
- **Sleep**: per the **AASM**, infants 4-12 mo need 12-16 hr, toddlers 1-2 yr 11-14 hr, preschoolers 3-5 yr 10-13 hr, school-age 6-12 yr **9-12 hr**, and teens 13-18 yr **8-10 hr**. Chronic short sleep is independently associated with higher BMI.
- **Sugar-sweetened beverages**: the single biggest dietary lever in most US pediatric cases. AHA recommends <25 g (6 tsp) of added sugar per day for ages 2-18 and **no added-sugar beverages under 2**.

faq.q: What is a healthy BMI percentile for my child?
faq.a: Per CDC, a **Healthy Weight** percentile is between the **5th and <85th** for the child's age and sex. There's no single 'healthy BMI number' — a BMI of 17 may be healthy for a 9-year-old girl but overweight for a 5-year-old boy. Always read BMI alongside the growth-chart percentile, not in isolation.

faq.q: Is the 95th percentile bad? My pediatrician used the word 'obesity' and it scared me.
faq.a: BMI ≥95th percentile meets the CDC definition of **obesity** in children, but the word is a clinical category, not a judgment. The 2023 AAP guideline reframed pediatric obesity as a **chronic disease** to be treated early — that means evidence-based options exist (intensive lifestyle treatment, and for adolescents ≥12, pharmacotherapy as adjunct). Ask your pediatrician about a referral to a pediatric weight management program if available locally.

faq.q: My child is below the 5th percentile — should I worry?
faq.a: Underweight in children can reflect a constitutionally lean build, late puberty, or an underlying issue (malabsorption, eating disorder, chronic illness, food insecurity). Look at the **trend**: a child tracking steadily along the 3rd percentile is usually fine; a child who has crossed downward through two percentile lines warrants evaluation. Bring the growth chart to your pediatrician — they'll consider history, exam, and possibly labs.

faq.q: Is BMI accurate for a muscular teenage athlete?
faq.a: BMI doesn't distinguish lean mass from fat mass, so muscular athletes can have an elevated BMI without true excess adiposity. In those cases, pediatricians use additional tools: **waist-to-height ratio > 0.5** as a simple screen, skinfold thickness, or body composition by bioimpedance/DEXA when available. If a teen has BMI ≥85th but normal waist circumference, a healthy diet, and good fitness, it's almost always muscle — not a problem.

faq.q: Is pediatric weight loss safe? Aren't kids supposed to grow?
faq.a: For most children with overweight, the goal isn't weight loss — it's **weight maintenance while height continues**, so the child 'grows into' a healthier BMI. For children with obesity, modest gradual weight loss can be appropriate under medical supervision. Never restrict calories in young children without pediatric guidance; their nutritional needs for growth are non-negotiable. Restrictive 'diets' are explicitly discouraged.

faq.q: Can a teenager get bariatric surgery?
faq.a: Yes — the 2023 AAP guideline supports referral for **metabolic and bariatric surgery in adolescents ≥13 years** with severe obesity (BMI ≥120% of the 95th percentile or ≥35 kg/m²), particularly when accompanied by significant comorbidities and after evaluation by a comprehensive multidisciplinary pediatric program. Outcomes data (e.g., Teen-LABS study) show durable weight loss and remission of type 2 diabetes and hypertension at 5 years.

faq.q: Can my child take Wegovy (semaglutide) for weight loss?
faq.a: **Semaglutide (Wegovy)** is FDA-approved for chronic weight management in adolescents **≥12 years** with obesity (BMI ≥95th percentile), as an adjunct to lifestyle treatment. The 2023 AAP guideline supports pharmacotherapy as part of comprehensive obesity treatment in this age range. Decisions should be made by a pediatrician familiar with pediatric obesity medicine — not based on adult prescribing patterns.

faq.q: How often should we re-check BMI?
faq.a: BMI is measured at every well-child visit in US primary care — typically annually from age 3 onward. The single most useful piece of information isn't any one number but the **trajectory** on the growth chart. A child who has crossed upward through two major percentile lines in a year deserves a closer look even if still within Healthy Weight range.

faq.q: Does this calculator use CDC or WHO percentile bands?
faq.a: There are two reference systems for ages 2-19. The **CDC** (US standard) sets overweight at the 85th percentile and obesity at the **95th**; the international **WHO BMI-for-age** reference sets overweight at the 85th (+1 SD) and obesity at about the **97th** (+2 SD). This calculator places the child's BMI on the **WHO 5th/85th/97th bands** for their age and sex, then shows the CDC weight-status categories above as the US reference. For a child sitting right on the 95th-97th boundary, ask which chart your pediatrician's EHR uses — the practical difference is small, and the **trend over time** matters more than a single reading.
